Explanation: The esophagus, stomach, liver, and pancreas develop from the embryonic foregut (their parenchymal/epithelial derivatives are endodermal). The spleen is correctly excluded because it arises from dorsal mesogastrium mesenchyme.
Source Section: Embryology / Gut Derivatives; Stomach / General Principles; Pancreas / General Principles; PDF pp. 3, 30, 116
Notes: Accurate; relationship is epithelial/parenchymal foregut origin, not all tissue layers. Board overlap: avoid a competing midgut/hindgut-derivative category on the same board. Verified against standard embryology (Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed.; Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed.).

Connection Title: Muscles of mastication supplied by CN V3
Explanation: These are the four muscles of mastication, all first pharyngeal arch derivatives that move the mandible and receive motor supply from the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: First pharyngeal arch muscles of mastication; Trigeminal (V3) motor muscles
Source Section: Oral Cavity / Pharyngeal Arch Derivatives of Mastication; PDF pp. 10
Notes: First-arch origin and V3 motor supply are concordant, mutually reinforcing descriptors (accepted alternate names), not competing categories. Verified against Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.

Connection Title: Tongue muscles innervated by CN XII
Explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) innervates all intrinsic tongue muscles and all extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus, which receives vagal (pharyngeal plexus) motor supply.
Source Section: Oral Cavity / Tongue and Gustation; PDF pp. 11
Notes: Medically accurate; palatoglossus (CN X) is the correct exclusion. Style caveat: Tile 4 is a collective category alongside three named muscles; acceptable as a distinct, non-alias tile but confirm it fits Plexus tile conventions. Verified against Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.

Connection Title: Systemic diseases associated with recurrent aphthous oral ulcers
Explanation: Each of these systemic conditions is associated with recurrent aphthous ulceration. Oral ulcers can occur in each but are not sufficient alone to diagnose any of them.
Source Section: Oral Cavity / Labial and Gingival Pathology; PDF pp. 12
Notes: IBD is used as an umbrella tile; do not also place a separate Crohn or UC tile on the same board. Association, not universal. Verified against Rogler et al., Gastroenterology 2021 (IBD oral aphthae) and Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Phenytoin, cyclosporine, and calcium channel blockers (classically nifedipine) cause drug-induced gingival hyperplasia; monocytic AML (FAB M4/M5) causes gingival enlargement from leukemic infiltration.
Source Section: Oral Cavity / Labial and Gingival Pathology; PDF pp. 12
Notes: Mixed category (three drug causes + one disease) is intentional and medically valid; risk varies by CCB agent and AML subtype (leukemic infiltration is most characteristic of monocytic subtypes). Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each can produce an enlarged tongue: soft-tissue overgrowth in acromegaly, myxedematous infiltration in hypothyroidism, amyloid deposition in amyloidosis, and congenital overgrowth in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
Source Section: Oral Cavity / Oral Mucosal Pathology; PDF pp. 13
Notes: Association, not a universal finding. Amyloidosis is the most common cause of acquired adult macroglossia; BWS causes true macroglossia in ~85%. Board overlap: Down syndrome also causes (relative) macroglossia. Verified: Simmonds et al., Cleft Palate Craniofac J 2018; Prada et al., Pediatrics 2012; Tabbarah et al., Neurology 2005.

Explanation: These oral medications cause direct caustic esophageal mucosal injury when a tablet/capsule has prolonged contact with the mucosa (inadequate water, recumbency).
Source Section: Esophagus / Esophagitis; PDF pp. 24
Notes: Classic pill-esophagitis quartet; effect is contact-dependent, not universal. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed. and Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed.

Explanation: Selective loss of inhibitory (NO/VIP) myenteric neurons produces incomplete LES relaxation and aperistalsis, causing dysphagia to both solids and liquids and the distal bird-beak tapering on barium esophagram.
Source Section: Esophagus / Esophageal Disorders of Motility; PDF pp. 22
Notes: Findings are characteristic, not individually pathognomonic; confirm with high-resolution manometry (elevated IRP) and exclude pseudoachalasia. Verified: ACG Achalasia Guideline 2020; Pandolfino & Gawron, JAMA 2015; Patel et al., Gastroenterology 2022.

Explanation: These promote GERD through distinct mechanisms: increased intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy), disruption of the gastroesophageal junction barrier (sliding hiatal hernia), and low LES tone/dysmotility (scleroderma).
Source Section: Esophagus / Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease; Additional Dysphagia-Related Pathology; PDF pp. 22-25
Notes: Do not retitle as conditions that all directly lower LES pressure, since mechanisms differ. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each mechanically narrows the esophageal lumen, classically producing solid-food dysphagia first; advanced carcinoma may progress to dysphagia for liquids as well.
Source Section: Esophagus / Additional Dysphagia-Related Pathology; Esophageal Malignancy; PDF pp. 25, 27
Notes: Distinguish mechanical dysphagia (solids first) from motility dysphagia (solids + liquids). Esophageal web is discussed under Plummer-Vinson. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Physiologic inhibitors of gastric acid secretion
Explanation: Somatostatin is the principal physiologic inhibitor of gastric acid; secretin inhibits acid via somatostatin and prostaglandin release; cholecystokinin inhibits acid largely by stimulating somatostatin; prostaglandin E2 directly inhibits parietal cells (EP3/Gi). The original GIP tile was replaced because GIP inhibits acid only at supraphysiologic doses and is not a physiologic inhibitor in humans.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Enterogastrones; Physiologic inhibitors of gastric H+ secretion
Source Section: Stomach / Gastric Regulation; Intestinal Regulation; Parietal Cell Physiology; PDF pp. 36, 38-39
Notes: REVISED: GIP replaced by cholecystokinin. GIP acid inhibition is a pharmacologic artifact (name changed from gastric inhibitory to glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide). Added refs: Baggio & Drucker, Gastroenterology 2007; Nauck et al., Digestion 1992; Meier et al., World J Gastroenterol 2006; Schubert & Rehfeld, Compr Physiol 2019; Chung et al., Gastroenterology 1994. Board overlap: shares secretin and CCK with GI-012; do not use both on one board.

Connection Title: Intestinal hormones that slow gastric emptying
Explanation: Secretin, CCK, peptide YY, and GLP-1 are intestinal ('ileal brake') hormones that slow gastric emptying, coordinating delivery of chyme with intestinal digestive capacity. The original GIP tile was replaced because controlled human studies show GIP does not slow gastric emptying and may slightly accelerate it.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Intestinal/ileal brake hormones; Hormones that delay gastric emptying
Source Section: Stomach / Intestinal Regulation; PDF pp. 38
Notes: REVISED: GIP replaced by peptide YY (PYY), a prototypical ileal-brake hormone. Added refs: Meier et al., Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2004; Edholm et al., Neurogastroenterol Motil 2010; Nauck & Meier, Diabetes Obes Metab 2018; Goyal et al., Neurogastroenterol Motil 2019 (gastric braking hormones). Board overlap: shares secretin and CCK with GI-011; do not use both on one board.

Connection Title: Gastrointestinal causes of vitamin B12 deficiency
Explanation: Each can cause B12 deficiency by a distinct GI mechanism: loss of intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), failure to cleave R-protein-B12 (pancreatic insufficiency), mucosal malabsorption +/- concomitant autoimmune gastritis (celiac disease), and luminal competition (D. latum).
Source Section: Stomach / Pernicious Anemia; PDF pp. 40
Notes: Preserve can cause wording. Celiac-related B12 deficiency is legitimate but less characteristic than iron/folate (terminal ileum relatively spared). Verified: Green et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017; Stabler, NEJM 2013; Allen et al., J Clin Invest 1978; Oxentenko & Murray, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2015.

Explanation: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causes loss of intrinsic factor (and B12 malabsorption) and oxyntic (body/fundic) atrophic gastritis, which carries increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and type 1 gastric carcinoid.
Source Section: Stomach / Pernicious Anemia; PDF pp. 40
Notes: Malignancy risk is increased, not inevitable. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed. and Toh et al., NEJM 1997.

Explanation: Excess TGF-alpha signaling drives foveolar (mucous-cell) hyperplasia and giant rugal folds with parietal-cell atrophy; mucosal protein loss produces protein-losing gastropathy and hypoalbuminemia.
Source Section: Stomach / Gastritis and Stress-related Mucosal Disease; PDF pp. 43
Notes: Board overlap: distinguish from other causes of enlarged gastric folds (ZES/GI-016, lymphoma) by histology/context. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: A gastrinoma causes marked hypergastrinemia and gastric acid hypersecretion with treatment-refractory/atypical peptic ulcers and diarrhea; ~25% of cases occur within MEN1. Fasting gastrin must be interpreted with gastric pH (<2).
Source Section: Stomach / Peptic Ulcer Disease; Pancreas / Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; PDF pp. 46, 132
Notes: MEN1 is an association (~25%), not a requirement; most are sporadic. Verified: Jensen & Metz, Yamada's Atlas of Gastroenterology 2022; Chatzipanagiotou et al., J Neuroendocrinol 2023; Lamberti et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024.

Explanation: Each irreversibly inhibits the parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase (gastric proton pump), covalently binding activated enzyme to suppress acid secretion.
Source Section: Stomach / Gastric Pharmacology; PDF pp. 49
Notes: -prazole suffix makes membership easy; mechanism gives educational value. Verified against Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed.

Connection Title: Nutrients at risk with prolonged PPI use
Explanation: Prolonged acid suppression is associated with reduced absorption/deficiency risk for iron, calcium, magnesium (hypomagnesemia is an FDA labeled warning), and vitamin B12. The group is correctly three minerals plus one vitamin.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nutrients affected by chronic acid suppression
Source Section: Stomach / Gastric Pharmacology; PDF pp. 49
Notes: Use nutrients (not minerals) in the title because B12 is a vitamin. Risk varies by nutrient, dose, duration. Verified against US FDA PPI labeling (hypomagnesemia) and Katzung, 15th ed.

Tile 4: Creatinine rise without true GFR loss
Explanation: Cimetidine inhibits hepatic CYP450, has antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia), causes CNS effects (confusion, especially in elderly/renal impairment), and raises serum creatinine by inhibiting its tubular secretion without reducing true GFR.
Source Section: Stomach / Gastric Pharmacology; PDF pp. 49
Notes: The creatinine effect is pseudo-renal dysfunction (inhibited tubular creatinine secretion). Verified against Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed.

Explanation: Zone 3 (centrilobular/pericentral) hepatocytes are most distal to oxygenated blood (ischemia-prone) and richest in CYP450 (generating toxic metabolites of acetaminophen and halothane); alcohol-related injury is also centrilobular.
Source Section: Liver / Hepatic Zones; Alcohol-induced Hepatitis; Additional Liver Pathologies; PDF pp. 59-60, 67
Notes: Zonal preference is not absolute; severe injury can extend. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Biallelic ATP7B defects impair hepatocyte copper export, causing low serum ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hour urinary copper, and corneal copper deposition (Kayser-Fleischer rings).
Source Section: Liver / Wilson Disease; PDF pp. 65
Notes: Characteristic, not mandatory: ceruloplasmin can be normal, and KF rings are absent in ~50% of hepatic presentations. Verified: Roberts & Schilsky, NEJM 2023; AASLD Wilson Disease Practice Guidance 2022; Bandmann et al., Lancet Neurol 2015.

Connection Title: Therapies that reduce copper burden in Wilson disease
Explanation: Chelators (penicillamine, trientine) promote urinary copper excretion; zinc salts induce enterocyte metallothionein to block copper uptake; dietary restriction reduces intake. All lower body copper burden.
Source Section: Liver / Wilson Disease; PDF pp. 65
Notes: Different roles/mechanisms; category does not imply interchangeability or simultaneous use. Verified against AASLD Wilson Disease Practice Guidance 2022.

Explanation: Primary iron overload produces high serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation (TSAT >=45% is the usual screening threshold) with a low/reduced TIBC. Ferritin is also an acute-phase reactant.
Source Section: Liver / Hereditary Hemochromatosis; PDF pp. 66
Notes: Board overlap: this lab pattern is shared by secondary iron overload (accepted alternate framing); reduced TIBC is typical but not universal. Verified: Cabrera et al., JAMA 2022; Powell et al., Lancet 2016; Kane et al., Am Fam Physician 2021.

Explanation: Iron deposition causes skin hyperpigmentation (bronze), pancreatic islet damage (diabetes - 'bronze diabetes'), myocardial iron loading (restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy), and pituitary/gonadal deposition (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).
Source Section: Liver / Hereditary Hemochromatosis; PDF pp. 66
Notes: Associations, not universal (penetrance is incomplete). Verified: Cabrera et al., JAMA 2022; Walter, JAMA 2022; Powell et al., Lancet 2016.

Connection Title: Measures used to remove/reduce excess iron
Explanation: Phlebotomy directly removes iron (first-line for HFE hemochromatosis); deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone are iron chelators (mainly for transfusional overload or when phlebotomy is unsuitable).
Source Section: Liver / Hereditary Hemochromatosis; PDF pp. 66
Notes: Do not imply interchangeable first-line roles: phlebotomy is first-line for HFE hemochromatosis, chelators primarily for transfusional overload. Verified against Kane et al., Am Fam Physician 2021 and Powell et al., Lancet 2016.

Connection Title: Markers of impaired synthetic/metabolic function in advanced cirrhosis
Explanation: Advanced hepatocellular failure impairs clotting-factor synthesis (prolonged PT/INR), albumin synthesis, gluconeogenesis/glycogen storage (hypoglycemia), and ammonia detoxification (hyperammonemia).
Source Section: Liver / Cirrhosis; PDF pp. 68-69
Notes: Qualifier: PT/INR reflects synthetic function, not net bleeding risk in cirrhosis (rebalanced hemostasis); not all abnormalities are present simultaneously. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Peripheral stigmata linked to cirrhotic hyperestrogenism
Explanation: Impaired hepatic estrogen metabolism (with reduced free testosterone) contributes to gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and hypogonadism in cirrhosis.
Source Section: Liver / Cirrhosis; PDF pp. 68-69
Notes: Hyperestrogenism contributes but is not the sole mechanism for every finding. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Elevated portal pressure dilates portosystemic collaterals (esophageal and anorectal varices, caput medusae) and causes congestive splenomegaly.
Source Section: Liver / Portal Hypertension; PDF pp. 71
Notes: Anorectal varices are portosystemic collaterals and are distinct from ordinary (non-portal) internal hemorrhoids; do not substitute hemorrhoids. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Causes of portal hypertension by site of obstruction
Explanation: These raise portal pressure at different sites: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis - sinusoidal; schistosomiasis - presinusoidal), and posthepatic (Budd-Chiari / hepatic vein outflow obstruction).
Source Section: Liver / Portal Hypertension; PDF pp. 71
Notes: Do not claim a uniformly elevated HVPG: HVPG is normal in prehepatic and presinusoidal causes. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from reduced UGT1A1 conjugation
Explanation: Each features reduced bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity - mild in Gilbert, near-absent in Crigler-Najjar type I, partial in type II, and developmentally immature in physiologic neonatal jaundice - producing indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
Source Section: Biliary System / Hereditary Hyperbilirubinemia; Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia; PDF pp. 88, 90
Notes: CN type I and II are distinct subtypes; physiologic neonatal jaundice also reflects increased RBC turnover and enterohepatic recycling. Board overlap: shares physiologic neonatal jaundice with GI-032. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each raises unconjugated bilirubin in neonates through immature clearance (physiologic), beta-glucuronidase-enhanced enterohepatic recycling (breast milk jaundice), dehydration/reduced stooling (suboptimal intake), or increased production (hemolytic disease).
Source Section: Biliary System / Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia; PDF pp. 90
Notes: Suboptimal-intake (early, breastfeeding-failure) jaundice is distinct from breast milk jaundice (later onset). Board overlap: shares physiologic neonatal jaundice with GI-031. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each is an inherited disorder of bilirubin metabolism: reduced conjugation (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar via UGT1A1) causing indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and impaired canalicular excretion/storage (Dubin-Johnson via MRP2/ABCC2, Rotor) causing direct hyperbilirubinemia.
Source Section: Biliary System / Hereditary Hyperbilirubinemia; PDF pp. 88
Notes: Do not label all four as UGT1A1 defects or all benign - Crigler-Najjar type I can cause kernicterus. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each promotes cholesterol-supersaturated bile or biliary stasis: obesity and estrogen increase biliary cholesterol secretion, fibrates increase biliary cholesterol excretion, and rapid weight loss mobilizes cholesterol and reduces gallbladder emptying.
Source Section: Biliary System / Cholelithiasis; PDF pp. 93
Notes: Risk factors, not universal. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Impaired bile flow raises conjugated bilirubin (jaundice, bilirubinuria/dark urine), reduces stercobilin delivery to stool (pale/acholic stools), and causes pruritus (bile acid/other retained pruritogens).
Source Section: Biliary System / Choledocholithiasis; Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis; Primary Biliary Cholangitis; PDF pp. 99, 104, 108
Notes: Cholestasis and biliary obstruction are related acceptable framings; pale stools generally require substantial/complete obstruction. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Imaging and examination clues to acute cholecystitis
Explanation: Cystic-duct obstruction and inflammation produce a positive Murphy sign, sonographic gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm) and pericholecystic fluid, and nonvisualization of the gallbladder on HIDA (cholescintigraphy).
Source Section: Biliary System / Acute Cholecystitis; PDF pp. 96
Notes: Individual ultrasound signs are nonspecific; HIDA nonvisualization is sensitive but requires correct timing and has false positives. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: PSC is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis and atypical perinuclear ANCA; multifocal intra- and extrahepatic strictures produce a 'beaded' cholangiogram, and concentric 'onion-skin' periductal fibrosis is the characteristic histology.
Source Section: Biliary System / Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis; PDF pp. 104
Notes: p-ANCA is nonspecific; onion-skin fibrosis is infrequent on biopsy (~14% in one series) but characteristic when present. Verified: AASLD PSC Guidance 2023; Ponsioen et al., Gastroenterology 2021; Yu et al., Hum Pathol 2024.

Explanation: PBC is characterized by antimitochondrial antibodies and lymphocytic destruction of small/medium interlobular bile ducts (florid duct lesion, often with granulomas); chronic cholestasis/hyperlipidemia can produce xanthelasma.
Source Section: Biliary System / Primary Biliary Cholangitis; PDF pp. 108
Notes: AMA-negative PBC exists (use PBC-specific ANA - anti-sp100/gp210); xanthelasma is neither required nor specific. Verified: Tanaka et al., Lancet 2024; Jalan-Sakrikar et al., Physiol Rev 2026.

Connection Title: Causes of acute pancreatitis beyond alcohol and gallstones
Explanation: These metabolic (triglycerides >=1000 mg/dL; hypercalcemia), infectious (mumps), and iatrogenic (post-ERCP) factors are recognized triggers of acute pancreatitis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Non-biliary, non-alcohol causes of acute pancreatitis
Source Section: Pancreas / Acute Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 123
Notes: Preserve direction: HYPERcalcemia is a cause, whereas HYPOcalcemia is a consequence/severity marker. Verified: Mederos et al., JAMA 2021; Forsmark et al., NEJM 2016; Trikudanathan et al., Gastroenterology 2024.

Explanation: Each is reported to cause drug-induced pancreatitis; evidence strength differs - didanosine and azathioprine have strong/definite associations, whereas thiazide and loop diuretics have weaker, more circumstantial evidence.
Source Section: Pancreas / Acute Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 123
Notes: A listed association does not prove causation in an individual; diuretic causality is weaker than didanosine/azathioprine. Verified: Steinberg & Tenner, NEJM 1994; Mederos et al., JAMA 2021; Szatmary et al., Drugs 2022.

Explanation: Local complications include pseudocyst and hemorrhagic (necrotizing) pancreatitis; systemic inflammatory response can cause ARDS and DIC.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Local and systemic complications of pancreatitis
Source Section: Pancreas / Complications of Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 124
Notes: Temporal qualifier: a pseudocyst (encapsulated collection) matures over ~4+ weeks, whereas ARDS/DIC occur early. Verified: Trikudanathan et al., Gastroenterology 2024 and Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Diagnostic pattern of chronic pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
Explanation: Advanced chronic pancreatitis shows ductal calcifications and parenchymal atrophy with low fecal elastase (exocrine insufficiency), while normal D-xylose testing indicates intact small-bowel mucosal absorption - distinguishing pancreatic from mucosal malabsorption.
Source Section: Pancreas / Chronic Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 127
Notes: Normal D-xylose assumes no coexisting mucosal disease; calcifications and low elastase are not universal. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed. and Yamada's Textbook of Gastroenterology, 7th ed.

Connection Title: Fat-soluble vitamins at risk in pancreatic fat malabsorption
Explanation: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency impairs luminal fat digestion and micelle formation, reducing absorption of the four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Source Section: Pancreas / Chronic Pancreatitis; Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma; PDF pp. 127-128
Notes: Fat-soluble vitamins (ADEK) is the equivalent accepted category name (not a competing category). Verified against Yamada's Textbook of Gastroenterology, 7th ed. (Vitamins and minerals).

Explanation: A pancreatic-head mass obstructs the common bile duct (painless obstructive jaundice; palpable nontender gallbladder = Courvoisier sign) and the pancreatic duct (double-duct sign); tumor-associated hypercoagulability produces migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome).
Source Section: Pancreas / Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma; PDF pp. 128
Notes: Trousseau is an association, not required; Courvoisier and double-duct signs are suggestive, not specific. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Each is a hormone-secreting (functional) pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor producing a characteristic clinical syndrome from insulin, glucagon, VIP, or somatostatin excess.
Source Section: Pancreas / Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; PDF pp. 132
Notes: Do not retitle as MEN1 tumors - MEN1 association is not equally strong across all four. Verified: Kawasaki et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol 2023; ENETS Guidance (Hofland et al., J Neuroendocrinol 2023); NCCN Neuroendocrine Tumors 2026.

Explanation: Autonomous glucagon secretion causes necrolytic migratory erythema, hyperglycemia/diabetes, catabolic weight loss, and a hypercoagulable state with venous thromboembolism (part of the 'glucagonoma syndrome').
Source Section: Pancreas / Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; PDF pp. 132
Notes: Verified: Kawasaki et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol 2023; Albers et al., Sci Rep 2024 (NME, diabetes, VTE, diarrhea, stomatitis, anemia).

Explanation: VIP-driven intestinal secretion causes profuse secretory watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and achlorhydria (WDHA / Verner-Morrison syndrome); weight loss accompanies the catabolic state.
Source Section: Pancreas / Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; PDF pp. 132
Notes: Weight loss is nonspecific; WDHA is the specific triad. Verified: Kawasaki et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol 2023; NCCN Neuroendocrine Tumors 2026.

Explanation: Excess somatostatin inhibits insulin (diabetes/hyperglycemia), gallbladder contraction and CCK (cholelithiasis), and pancreatic exocrine secretion (steatorrhea), with accompanying weight loss.
Source Section: Pancreas / Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors; PDF pp. 132
Notes: Board overlap: steatorrhea/weight loss overlap with other GI syndromes - keep the full triad distinct. Verified: Kawasaki et al., Nat Rev Clin Oncol 2023; Tomassetti et al., Ann Oncol 2002; NCCN 2026.

Connection Title: Epithelial cell populations present in intestinal crypts
Explanation: Small-intestinal crypts contain stem cells and Paneth cells (crypt-restricted) plus goblet and enteroendocrine cells, contributing to renewal, antimicrobial defense, mucus, and hormone signaling.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Histology; PDF pp. 139
Notes: Title says present in (not confined to): Paneth and stem cells are crypt-restricted, whereas goblet and enteroendocrine cells also populate villi. Verified against standard histology (Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.).

Connection Title: Malabsorption disorders causing enteric hyperoxaluria (calcium oxalate stones)
Explanation: Fat malabsorption from each disorder leaves unabsorbed fatty acids to bind luminal calcium; free oxalate is then hyperabsorbed in the colon, causing enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. The original Whipple disease tile was replaced because no source directly links it to hyperoxaluria/oxalate stones.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Celiac Disease; Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth; Large Intestine / Crohn Disease; Pancreas / Chronic Pancreatitis; PDF pp. 127, 151, 155, 173
Notes: REVISED: Whipple disease replaced by chronic pancreatitis (a classic, well-documented cause). Crohn and celiac are strongly supported; SIBO is moderately supported (explicitly named as causing oxalate stones in GI literature). Added refs: Coe et al., NEJM 1992; Ermer et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2023; Bargagli et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025; Ciacci et al., J Urol 2008 (celiac); Dibaise et al., Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2006 (SIBO oxalate stones). Board overlap: do not co-list with short bowel syndrome/RYGB as a competing enteric-hyperoxaluria set.

Explanation: Gluten-triggered immune injury produces positive anti-tTG IgA serology and the characteristic duodenal histology: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Celiac Disease; PDF pp. 151
Notes: Caveats: IgA deficiency causes false-negative tTG-IgA (check total IgA / use IgG-based tests); serology/histology can normalize on a gluten-free diet; histology is not entirely specific. Verified: Oxentenko & Murray, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2015; Kelly et al., Gastroenterology 2015.

Explanation: Disseminated Tropheryma whipplei infection affects joints (often preceding GI symptoms by years), heart (blood culture-negative endocarditis), lymph nodes, and CNS, in addition to malabsorption.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Whipple Disease; PDF pp. 154
Notes: Neurologic dysfunction is a broad tile; consider oculomasticatory myorhythmia/ophthalmoplegia if board-level overlap is excessive. Verified: Marth et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016; Bai et al., Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2004.

Explanation: Loss-of-function MTP (MTTP) prevents assembly/secretion of ApoB-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL), causing fat malabsorption with lipid-laden enterocytes, very low plasma lipids, acanthocytosis, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Additional Malabsorption Syndromes; PDF pp. 157
Notes: Correct framing: the primary defect is impaired particle assembly (MTTP), not an APOB gene mutation. Verified against GeneReviews / standard biochemistry (Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.).

Explanation: Each can act as a lead point around which proximal bowel telescopes into distal bowel - a structural lesion (Meckel diverticulum, tumor, polyp) or lymphoid hypertrophy (enlarged Peyer patches, often post-viral in children).
Source Section: Small Intestine / Intussusception; PDF pp. 161
Notes: Enlarged Peyer patches are a functional (not discrete mass) lead point typical of pediatric ileocolic intussusception; most childhood cases are idiopathic. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Telescoping bowel causes episodic colicky pain and a palpable sausage-shaped mass; venous congestion and mucosal sloughing produce currant-jelly stool, and concentric bowel layers create the ultrasound target sign.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Intussusception; PDF pp. 161
Notes: The complete classic triad is often absent; currant-jelly stool is a later (ischemic) sign. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: When serotonin and other vasoactive amines reach the systemic circulation (classically via hepatic metastases bypassing first-pass metabolism), they cause flushing, secretory diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided valvular (tricuspid/pulmonary) fibrosis.
Source Section: Small Intestine / Carcinoid Tumor; PDF pp. 162
Notes: Right-sided valve disease is classic (left-sided in ~10-15%, e.g., with PFO or bronchial primary). Verified: Maleszewski et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2018; Vijayvergia et al., Gastroenterology 2026; NCCN Neuroendocrine Tumors 2026.

Explanation: Discontinuous (skip) and transmural inflammation accounts for the segmental gross pattern, mesenteric fat wrapping (creeping fat), noncaseating granulomas (when present), and penetrating complications such as fistulas.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Crohn Disease; PDF pp. 173
Notes: Noncaseating granulomas are characteristic but present in a minority of biopsies. Verified: Caruso et al., Nat Rev Immunol 2020; Chang, NEJM 2020.

Explanation: UC causes continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally, with neutrophilic crypt abscesses, regenerative inflammatory pseudopolyps, and loss of haustra ('lead-pipe' colon) in chronic disease.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Ulcerative Colitis; PDF pp. 176
Notes: Lead-pipe appearance is a chronic finding; treatment can produce patchy/relative rectal sparing. Verified: Caruso et al., Nat Rev Immunol 2020; Neurath, Nat Rev Immunol 2014.

Connection Title: Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease
Explanation: These musculoskeletal (enteropathic arthritis), ocular (uveitis), and cutaneous (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum) manifestations occur in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Crohn Disease; Ulcerative Colitis; PDF pp. 173, 176
Notes: Board overlap: these findings also occur outside IBD (e.g., sarcoidosis, spondyloarthropathy) - avoid a competing systemic-inflammatory category on the same board. Verified: Rogler et al., Gastroenterology 2021; Khrom et al., Gastroenterology 2024.

Explanation: Each can obstruct the appendiceal lumen, causing secretion retention, rising intraluminal pressure, venous/arterial compromise, and acute appendicitis.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Appendicitis; PDF pp. 180
Notes: Lymphoid hyperplasia (children) and fecalith (adults) are most common; neoplasm and foreign body are less frequent; luminal obstruction is not demonstrable in every case. Verified against Robbins & Cotran, 10th ed.

Explanation: Failed craniocaudal migration of enteric neural crest cells leaves the distal rectum/colon aganglionic and tonically contracted, causing functional obstruction, delayed meconium passage (>48 h), and dilation of the proximal ganglionic bowel (megacolon).
Source Section: Large Intestine / Hirschsprung Disease; PDF pp. 186
Notes: Diagnosis confirmed by rectal biopsy (aganglionosis, hypertrophied nerve trunks); RET mutations are most common. Verified: Montalva et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2023; Westfal & Goldstein, NeoReviews 2018.

Connection Title: Autosomal dominant hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes
Explanation: Each is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and increases colorectal (and extracolonic) cancer risk via distinct pathways: MMR deficiency (Lynch), APC adenomatous polyposis (FAP), STK11 hamartomas (Peutz-Jeghers), and SMAD4/BMPR1A juvenile polyps (JPS).
Source Section: Large Intestine / Colorectal Cancer; Polyposis Syndromes; PDF pp. 197, 199
Notes: Lynch is the nonpolyposis member; MUTYH-associated polyposis is correctly excluded (autosomal recessive). Verified: Mao et al., ACMG 2021; Monahan et al., Gastroenterology 2025; Boardman et al., AGA 2020.

Explanation: Gardner syndrome (an APC-related FAP phenotype) features extracolonic manifestations: osteomas (especially mandible/skull), desmoid tumors, epidermoid (sebaceous) cysts, and dental anomalies (supernumerary/impacted teeth), in addition to adenomatous colonic polyposis.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Polyposis Syndromes; PDF pp. 199
Notes: Gardner syndrome = FAP with extracolonic features (also CHRPE). Verified: Hegde et al., ACMG 2014; Mankaney et al., ACG 2026.

Explanation: Each draws water into the bowel lumen by an osmotic effect (poorly absorbed magnesium salts, PEG, and nonabsorbable lactulose), softening stool and promoting evacuation.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Anticonstipation Medications; PDF pp. 200
Notes: Board overlap: magnesium hydroxide also acts as an antacid - avoid a conflicting antacid category. Lactulose additionally lowers ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy. Verified against Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed.

Explanation: Each blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors centrally (area postrema/CTZ) and peripherally (vagal afferents) to prevent nausea/vomiting, especially chemotherapy-induced.
Source Section: Large Intestine / Antiemetic Medications; PDF pp. 202
Notes: Do not label all four as equally QT-prolonging; palonosetron (longer half-life, second generation) has a different profile. Verified against Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed.

Connection Title: Clues to congenital indirect inguinal hernia
Tile 3: Entry through the deep (internal) inguinal ring
Explanation: A persistent (patent) processus vaginalis allows an indirect hernia sac to enter the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and traverse the inguinal canal; the same patency underlies a communicating hydrocele.
Source Section: Hernias / Indirect and Direct Inguinal Hernias; PDF pp. 206
Notes: Category is scoped to the congenital form (patent processus vaginalis); not all indirect hernias are congenital. Contrast with direct hernias (medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through Hesselbach triangle). Verified against Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.
